blocks.text: I shall add, as a corollary, the causes that the Hebrews devise for this plague, inflicted by God on the murmuring people. Aben Ezra observes that in Eccles. X, 11. בעל לשון, that is, the slanderer or blasphemer, is compared by Solomon with a serpent that bites when it is not charmed. From this he infers that the biting of an insolent tongue among the Israelite people was justly punished by the bite of serpents. And perhaps this is not beside the point. For in Psal. CXL, 4. too, slanderers are said to sharpen their tongue like serpents, and to have the poison of asps under their lips. But the Jerusalem translator, largely following Jonathan, seems to offer mere trifles in his paraphrase of Num. XXI, 6. A daughter of the voice (he says, that is, an oracle) went forth from the midst of the earth, and a voice was heard on high: namely, See, all you sons of men, and listen; and hear, all you sons of flesh. I cursed the serpent from the foundation of the world, and said to it, „Dust shall be your food“. Yet it did not murmur on account of its food. But my people (the Israelites) I led out free from Egypt, and sent down to them Manna from heaven, and brought quails over from the sea, and raised up for them a well from the abyss. Yet again they murmur against me on account of the Manna, saying that their soul is distressed because of the bread, whose eating is light. Therefore the serpent shall come, which did not murmur on account of its food; and I will make it bite the people of those who murmured on account of their food. And the word of the Lord stirred up against the people burning serpents, etc. As if it were to be counted to the serpent's praise that it does not murmur against God, whom it does not know.

Our own interpreters also look for allegories here: by the bites of the burning serpents they understand the fiery darts of Satan of Ephes. VI, 16., that is, the wicked suggestions by which he kindles the heat of lust, inflicts various wounds on us, and spreads his poison through all parts of the soul. Further, just as serpents are sent against the Israelites for their contempt of the manna and their murmuring against God and Moses, Num. XXI, 5. 6., so those are deservedly handed over to Satan who neglect the word of God, signified by the manna, or who blaspheme God himself, like Hymenaeus and Alexander 1 Tim. I, 20. But just as those Israelites for whom, unconcerned about a remedy, the serpents' bites were deadly are a figure of the impenitent, who, spurning the grace of God, die in their sins, so those who flee to Moses, confessing their sins and imploring the grace of God, Num. XXI, 7., plainly signify those whom the sense of their sins and the fear of divine judgment move to sounder counsels: such as those who, pricked in their heart, say to Peter and the rest of the Apostles, What shall we do, men and brethren? Act. II, 37., and the jailer of Philippi, [III, 218] who, falling trembling at the feet of Paul and Silas, says, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? Actor. XVI, 29. 30. For their sake God commanded Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole, and promised that all who had been bitten by serpents would be healed at the sight of it. The outcome confirmed this. Nor is there any doubt that that serpent foreshadowed Christ. For so Christ himself asserts, Iohan. III, 14.: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up. Many people give many reasons for the type. For instance, first, that the serpent had the form of the serpents that burned with their bite, yet not their poison, just as Christ was in the likeness of sinful flesh, Roman. VIII, 3., though free from sin. Second, that the serpent was of bronze, not gold, and cast from a baser metal, so as to show us Christ, in whom there was no form, nor comeliness, nor any beauty, that we should desire him, Es. LIII, 2. Third, that the divine strength of Christ is signified by the firmness and durability of bronze. Hence Iob. VI, 12.: Is my strength the strength of stones? Is my flesh of bronze? And the Poet:
I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze. [col. 426]
Fourth, of all metals bronze is the most resonant. Hence Paul, 1 Cor. XIII, 1.: γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν [gegona chalkos ēchōn]. And Claudian:
No Corybant of Cybele purified you at your birth with sounding bronze. — — —
